events.title: McCulloch & Pitts neuron logic
events.summary: McCulloch and Pitts argue that because a neuron either fires or does not, the activity of a nervous net can be written as propositional logic. Any net can be described as logical expressions, and any logical expression meeting certain conditions can be built as a net. They treat the physiological details they cannot settle (how inhibition works, whether refractoriness is relative or absolute, how learning alters a net) as immaterial, because for each such assumption an equivalent net exists that gives the same result. They then draw large conclusions: nets with circles compute what a Turing machine computes, and mental activity is "rigorously deduceable from present neurophysiology."
events.sourceNote: McCulloch and Pitts - A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity

events.title: Wiener's Cybernetics
events.summary: In the Introduction, dated Mexico City, November 1947, Norbert Wiener names a new field. He and his collaborators had found "the essential unity" of problems of communication, control and statistical mechanics "whether in the machine or in living tissue," and they coined "Cybernetics," from the Greek for steersman, to cover it. The Introduction traces the field's origin to wartime work on anti-aircraft fire prediction and feedback, to physiology with Arturo Rosenblueth, and to mathematical logic and the new computing machines. It ends with a warning. Automatic control will produce a second industrial revolution that devalues routine human judgment, and the scientists who built the field stand in an uncomfortable moral position in a world "of Belsen and Hiroshima."
events.sourceNote: Cybernetics - Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine

events.title: Hebb's Organization of Behavior
events.summary: Hebb's book proposes a single neurophysiological theory for perception, learning and thought. Its three main ideas, as Brown summarizes them, are the "Hebb synapse" (cells repeatedly active together become associated, so that activity in one facilitates the other), the cell assembly (a group of neurons wired into closed loops by perceptual learning, which can keep firing after a stimulus stops and so becomes the basis for thought), and the phase sequence (a series of cell assemblies that amounts to a train of thought). Hebb himself later described the aim as dealing with set, attention, perceptual generalization and learning "in one theoretical framework," and called his the only attempt to treat thought and perception inside a theory of learning.

events.title: Turing's imitation game
events.summary: replaced "can machines think?" with an agreed behavioural criterion

events.title: Dartmouth proposal names the field
events.summary: named the field in a funding proposal
events.sourceNote: A PROPOSAL FOR THE DARTMOUTH SUMMER RESEARCH PROJECTON ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

events.title: Logic Theorist
events.summary: Newell and Simon specify a system, the logic theorist (LT), that discovers proofs for theorems in the propositional calculus of Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica. Their interest is less in logic than in a class of systems they call "complex information processing systems": systems with many kinds of processes, used contingently on earlier results and reused hierarchically and recursively. Ordinary computer programs, they argue, run a few simple subroutines systematically; they call those algorithms and contrast them with heuristic methods, which LT relies on. LT offers no guarantee of finding a proof. The paper gives the complete specification in a pseudo-code, the logic language (LL), and leaves the computer implementation to later papers.

events.title: Rosenblatt's perceptron
events.summary: Rosenblatt presents the perceptron as "a hypothetical nervous system, or machine" built to show how information could be stored and used for recognition without a coded, one-to-one memory. He takes the "connectionist" position: what a system retains is held in connections between randomly wired units, not in stored images. Rather than symbolic logic, he describes the system with probability theory, and argues that its learning and discrimination can be predicted from six measurable physical parameters. He claims this is "the first actual completion" of a bridge between neurophysiology and psychology, something he says Hebb had suggested but never built.
events.sourceNote: The Perceptron - A Probabilistic Model for Information Storage and Organization in the Brain

events.title: Mechanisation of Thought conference
events.summary: The proceedings record a four-day symposium at the National Physical Laboratory in Teddington, 24–27 November 1958, built on the premise that several separate specialties shared one subject. The preface lists them: artificial thinking, character and pattern recognition, learning, mechanical language translation, biology, automatic programming, industrial planning and clerical mechanization. The organizers felt the common theme was the mechanization of thought processes and that specialists in each would gain from meeting. In his opening address, NPL director G. B. B. M. Sutherland states the laboratory's own interest plainly: its Control Mechanisms and Electronics Division wanted to build equipment for routine mental work then done by large numbers of people. The first paper, Marvin Minsky's, declines to define intelligence at all and proposes heuristic programming as the working method.

events.title: McCarthy's Lisp paper
events.summary: McCarthy reports that the Artificial Intelligence group at MIT has built a programming system, LISP (for LISt Processor), on the IBM 704. It was designed as the tool for a proposed program, the Advice Taker, that would take declarative as well as imperative sentences and show "common sense" in carrying out instructions. In development the system was simplified until it rested on a mathematical scheme: a class of symbolic expressions (S-expressions) and recursive functions over them (S-functions). McCarthy therefore presents LISP as a formalism first, independent of any particular computer, and claims it serves both as a programming language and as a basis for a theory of computation.
events.sourceNote: Recursive Functions of Symbolic Expressions and Their Computation by Machine

events.title: Unimate enters GM production
events.summary: Both sources tell the same story: in 1961 General Motors put the first Unimate, a hydraulic, programmable arm built by Unimation, to work in a New Jersey plant unloading hot metal castings from a die-casting machine. It is presented as the first successful application of an industrial robot. The sources trace it to George Devol's 1954 patent for a "programmed article transfer" device and to Joseph Engelberger's work in financing and selling it. The Spectrum article adds the commercial and labor history: GM bought the first machine below cost, Unimation took years to turn a profit, American workers later protested robot-heavy lines, and the technology found its main early market in Japan.

events.title: DENDRAL begins
events.summary: The National Library of Medicine's essay presents DENDRAL, begun at Stanford in 1965, as "a prototype for expert systems and the first use of artificial intelligence in biomedical research." Joshua Lederberg, Edward Feigenbaum and Carl Djerassi built a program that inferred the molecular structure of unknown organic compounds from mass-spectrometer data. The essay argues that DENDRAL's main significance was theoretical: it moved AI from chess and other controlled settings to real scientific problems, and it forced its builders to formalize expert reasoning. It is equally direct about the limits. Expert systems were costly, narrow and slow to build, never replaced the scientist or physician, and struggled to win acceptance from the professionals they were meant to help.

events.title: Weizenbaum's ELIZA
events.summary: Joseph Weizenbaum of MIT describes ELIZA, a program on the MAC time-sharing system that holds typed conversations in natural language. It works by finding keywords in the user's sentence and applying decomposition and reassembly rules to produce a reply. The rules live in a separate "script," so the program is not tied to one set of responses or even one language. Weizenbaum's stated aim is to explain the program so plainly that it loses its apparent intelligence. His discussion argues that ELIZA shows "how easy it is" to create the illusion of understanding, that people readily credit machine output with judgment, and that a useful conversational program would have to reveal its misunderstanding instead of hiding it.
events.sourceNote: ELIZA - A Computer Program For the Study of Natural Language Communication

events.title: SRI's Shakey the Robot
events.summary: SRI and the IEEE present Shakey as the first mobile robot able to perceive and reason about its surroundings. Built at Stanford Research Institute's Artificial Intelligence Center from 1966 to 1972, it could, in the IEEE citation's words, "perceive its surroundings, infer implicit facts from explicit ones, create plans, recover from errors in plan execution, and communicate using ordinary English." The IEEE nomination argues that its layered software, vision, planning and navigation methods became models for later robots and for consumer technology.

events.title: ALPAC report
events.summary: A committee of the National Academy of Sciences, chaired by John R. Pierce of Bell Labs, was asked to advise the Department of Defense, the CIA and the National Science Foundation on machine translation research. It concludes that there has been no machine translation of general scientific text and "none is in immediate prospect." It finds that the government has no shortage of human translators, that postedited machine output is slower and no cheaper than human translation, and that the main value of a decade of machine translation work has been to linguistics. It recommends funding computational linguistics as a science, judged on scientific merit, and funding practical, short-range work to make human translation faster and cheaper, including with machine aids.

events.title: Minsky & Papert's Perceptrons
events.summary: Minsky and Papert argue that the perceptron had been promoted without a mathematical account of what it could and could not do, and they set out to supply one. As Bottou summarizes, they hold that "the only scientific way" to know whether a perceptron can perform a task is to prove it, and they analyze specific geometric tasks such as parity and connectedness. Their results, in Bottou's phrase, do "not make the perceptron look very good": for example, no finite-order perceptron can represent the connectedness predicate. In the 1988 edition they restated the position that progress had stopped for lack of basic theory.
events.sourceNote: Perceptrons - An Introduction to Computational Geometry

events.title: Intel 4004: a calculator chip becomes a computer
events.summary: Intel 4004, built for a calculator
events.sourceNote: Computer, A History of the Information Machine “The Shaping of the Personal Computer”

events.title: Winograd's SHRDLU
events.summary: Winograd's dissertation describes SHRDLU, a program that holds a dialog in English about a small world of toy blocks. It answers questions, carries out commands and accepts new information, and it asks for clarification when it cannot resolve a sentence. The argument is that a computer cannot handle language well unless it understands the subject under discussion, so syntax, semantics and reasoning must be combined in one system rather than run in sequence. Winograd's specific method is to represent knowledge as procedures, programs that can call on each other, rather than as tables of rules or lists of patterns.

events.title: MYCIN at Stanford
events.summary: MYCIN was a Stanford program that advised physicians on the diagnosis and antibiotic treatment of infectious diseases. Its builders, Bruce Buchanan and Edward Shortliffe, looking back in 1984, present it as an experiment testing whether "a rule-based formalism was sufficient" for an expert consultation system that performs well, can be changed easily, and can be understood. They say the answer was yes, and call it "one of the best-known lessons in the history of AI." The National Library of Medicine's exhibit on Joshua Lederberg places MYCIN among Stanford's expert-system projects and records their limits: they were costly to build, confined to narrow domains, and met skepticism from the physicians they were meant to help.

events.title: Lighthill Report
events.summary: Lighthill, an applied mathematician from outside the field, was asked by the UK Science Research Council (SRC) for a personal view of AI. He divides the field into three categories: A, Advanced Automation (replacing people with machines for specific industrial or military tasks); C, Computer-based studies of the central nervous system (theory in neurobiology and psychology); and B, a "Bridge" category whose core is Building Robots. He judges A and C to have respectable if limited achievements, and B to have failed. Because the case for AI as "a continuous, coherent field" depends on category B, he concludes the field has not proved its unity and predicts its "fission" over the next 25 years.

events.title: Stanford Cart crosses a room
events.summary: Earnest, a former executive officer of the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Lab (SAIL), tells the history of one machine over 46 years. The Stanford Cart began as a NASA-related testbed for driving a Moon rover from Earth, was taken over by SAIL as a robot road vehicle for research on visual navigation, and in 1979, under Hans Moravec, "successfully crossed a chair-filled room without human intervention in about five hours." Earnest traces a line from the cart through SAIL's later robot vehicle Stanley to the Google driverless car.

events.title: AAAI founded
events.summary: Raj Reddy, a founder and later president of AAAI, explains why American AI researchers created their own scientific society in 1979. Through the 1970s the only regular meeting for the field was the biennial International Joint Conference on AI (IJCAI), run by volunteer faculty. After organizing IJCAI-77 and IJCAI-79, Reddy concluded the community needed "an enduring administrative mechanism and institutional memory" of the kind the IEEE and ACM provided. Joining an existing society was possible, he writes, but "the time and the effort needed to get them to accept AI was too daunting." The article describes how the society was named, financed and governed, and what its first conference (AAAI-80, at Stanford) contained.

events.title: Fukushima's neocognitron
events.summary: Fukushima, working at the NHK Broadcasting Science Research Laboratories in Tokyo, proposes a multilayer neural network that learns to recognize visual patterns regardless of where they appear. Earlier models, including his own 1975 cognitron, responded differently to the same pattern at different positions. The neocognitron fixes this with a structure taken from Hubel and Wiesel's hierarchy model of the visual cortex: alternating layers of "S-cells," which extract features and have modifiable input synapses, and "C-cells," which pool over nearby S-cells with fixed connections so that a small shift in the input does not change their response. The network organizes itself without a teacher, from repeated presentation of stimulus patterns. Fukushima frames the work first as a model of the brain and second as an answer to a practical problem in optical character reading.

events.title: R1/XCON: expert systems go commercial
events.summary: McDermott describes R1, a rule-based program built with Digital Equipment Corporation to configure VAX computer orders: turning a customer's order into a complete, valid set of components and how they fit together. The paper presents expert knowledge as something that can be captured in a large set of if-then rules, and treats R1's use in daily business at DEC as proof that this works in practice.
events.sourceNote: "R1 - A Rule-Based Configurer of Computer Systems"

events.title: Japan's Fifth Generation project
events.summary: Feigenbaum and Shrobe, two American AI researchers who visited ICOT in 1992 on a JTEC assessment committee, evaluate Japan's national Fifth Generation Computer Systems project ten years in. The government launched it in 1982 to build a new generation of "intelligent" computers for the economy and society, run through a central institute, ICOT, staffed by the Japanese computer manufacturers. The authors argue that the harsh verdicts of the early 1990s were "unrealistically negative": the hardware and software met their planned performance, and the project trained a generation of Japanese computer engineers. They also judge that the broad goal of useful intelligent applications was not met. Applications stayed at the demonstration stage, and ICOT's bet on logic programming in Prolog, outside the mainstream, left the manufacturers disenchanted.

events.title: DARPA Strategic Computing
events.summary: DARPA's Strategic Computing program set out to reach machine intelligence by advancing a whole research front at once. Salisbury describes the plan as a pyramid: microelectronics and computer architecture at the base, AI applications for the military in the middle, and generic machine intelligence at the top, all driven by large gains in computing power from linking many processors. Between 1983 and 1993 DARPA spent over $1 billion on it. Salisbury's verdict is that the program "over-promised and under-delivered" and faded into obscurity by the early 1990s, while producing narrower successes.

events.title: gap — expert systems, AI winter
events.summary: the vault's only available case of momentum failing

events.title: Backpropagation popularized
events.summary: The paper shows that a multi-layer neural network can learn useful internal representations by propagating output errors backward through its layers and adjusting weights by gradient descent. Its historical importance is less the invention of the method than its framing: hidden units could discover features on their own, answering the objection that neural networks could not learn anything a single-layer perceptron could not.

events.title: Lisp machine market collapse
events.summary: Lisp machines were computers built to run the Lisp language efficiently, the preferred language of US AI research. They grew out of MIT's AI Lab in the 1970s, were commercialized by Symbolics, Lisp Machines Inc. (LMI), Texas Instruments and Xerox, and served the expert-system boom of the early 1980s. In 1987, according to the "AI winter" article, the market for specialized Lisp-based AI hardware collapsed, because general-purpose workstations and later desktop computers could run Lisp well enough. "An entire industry worth half a billion dollars was replaced in a single year." By the early 1990s most Lisp machine companies had failed or left the field.

events.title: Pearl's Bayesian networks
events.summary: Pearl's book brought together his work of the early and mid-1980s on reasoning under uncertainty with probability. Its central tool is the Bayesian network: a probability model defined by a directed acyclic graph, in which conditional independence keeps the number of parameters manageable and allows distributed inference ("belief propagation"). Russell, writing the ACM profile, describes the book as combining "Pearl's philosophy, his theories of human cognition, and all his technical material into a persuasive whole that sparked a revolution in the field of artificial intelligence."

events.title: Watkins's Q-learning
events.summary: Watkins's thesis asks how animals could learn efficient behaviour from rewards and punishments, and answers with a family of algorithms built as "incremental dynamic programming." The central one, one-step Q-learning, lets an agent store a value for each action in each state and adjust those values from experience alone, without a model of its environment and without remembering more than the last step. Watkins claims the method works, gives a proof in an appendix, and says the idea is simple enough that he doubts nobody has thought of it before. The 1992 note with Peter Dayan states the convergence proof in full and names the method as "model-free reinforcement learning."

events.title: LeCun's ZIP-code convnet
events.summary: A team at AT&T Bell Laboratories argues that a learning network generalizes much better when knowledge about the task is built into its architecture. They apply this to handwritten ZIP-code digits from the U.S. Postal Service. A single network, trained by backpropagation directly on 16-by-16 pixel images, learns the whole recognition task from the normalized image to the final digit. The first layers are constrained to share weights and act as convolutions, so the network learns its own feature detectors rather than using hand-designed ones. The authors report results they consider state of the art for digit recognition, and a working system that runs the trained network on a commercial signal-processing chip.
events.sourceNote: Backpropagation Applied to Handwritten Zip Code Recognition

events.title: TD-Gammon
events.summary: Tesauro describes TD-Gammon, a neural network that learns to evaluate backgammon positions by playing against itself and learning from the outcomes, using a temporal difference (TD) method, TD(λ), from the class of methods named by Sutton. He says the program was built to test ideas in reinforcement learning rather than to win at backgammon, but it ended up far stronger than earlier programs and close to the best human players. His claim is that a learner starting with no built-in knowledge, given a nonlinear function approximator and a method for assigning delayed credit, can reach expert judgment, and that this makes TD methods "much more powerful than previously suspected."

events.title: Support-vector networks
events.summary: Cortes and Vapnik, at AT&T Labs-Research, present the support-vector network as "a new learning machine" for two-class problems. It maps inputs into a very high-dimensional feature space and draws a linear boundary there, chosen to leave the widest margin between classes. Only the few training points on that margin, the support vectors, determine the boundary, which the authors argue is why it generalizes well even in a space with billions of dimensions. Earlier work had covered data that can be separated without errors; this paper adds "soft margins" for data that cannot, and tests the result on handwritten digits against decision trees and neural networks.

events.title: Deep Blue defeats Kasparov
events.summary: The builders' own account describes Deep Blue as a massively parallel search system: a general-purpose IBM supercomputer combined with hundreds of custom chess chips, able to evaluate hundreds of millions of positions per second. The paper presents its win as the result of specialized hardware, search, and a hand-tuned evaluation function, not as a machine that "thinks" about chess the way people do.

events.title: Long Short-Term Memory
events.summary: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber argue that recurrent neural networks, which could in principle remember past inputs, fail in practice to learn dependencies across long gaps in time. Using Hochreiter's 1991 analysis, they show why: error signals sent backwards through time either blow up or shrink exponentially. Their remedy is a new architecture, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), built around memory cells whose internal state carries error unchanged over time (the "constant error carrousel"), guarded by multiplicative gates that learn when to let information in and out. They claim LSTM can bridge time lags of more than 1,000 steps, learns faster than competing methods, and solves artificial tasks no earlier recurrent method had solved.

events.title: The PageRank paper
events.summary: Page, Brin, Motwani and Winograd propose PageRank, "a method for rating Web pages objectively and mechanically," computed from the link structure of the Web. A page ranks high if the pages linking to it rank high, so one link from a major page can count for more than many links from obscure ones. The authors model this as a "random surfer" clicking links and occasionally jumping elsewhere, show that the calculation converges quickly on hundreds of millions of links, and test it in a search engine they built called Google. The paper's subtitle states the aim: to bring order to a web too large and uneven for older retrieval methods.

events.title: LeNet-5 and MNIST
events.summary: LeCun and colleagues at AT&T Labs-Research argue that pattern recognition systems improve when they rely more on automatic learning and less on hand-designed heuristics. They make the case in two steps. First, on a new benchmark of handwritten digits, MNIST, convolutional neural networks that learn their own features from pixels beat every other method they test. Second, whole document-reading systems can be trained end to end with Graph Transformer Networks instead of being assembled from separately designed modules. The paper ends in a deployed product: a check reader built around LeNet-5 that reads millions of checks.
events.sourceNote: Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition

events.title: Breiman's random forests
events.summary: Breiman, a statistician at Berkeley, defines a random forest as a collection of decision trees, each grown with its own independently drawn random element, which then vote on the answer. He proves that as trees are added the forest's error converges to a limit, so the method does not overfit, and he bounds that error by two quantities: how accurate the individual trees are and how correlated they are with each other. Forests that pick a random subset of features at each split, he reports, match or beat Adaboost, the leading method of the time, while being more robust to noise, faster, and able to estimate their own error and the importance of each input.

events.title: iRobot's Roomba launches
events.summary: iRobot announces Roomba Intelligent FloorVac, which it calls the first automatic floor vacuum sold in the United States, and a new consumer robotics division to make it. The company says it is applying "artificial intelligence technology and cost effective manufacturing" to household appliances, and that at $199.95 the product brings "advanced navigation technology" within reach of ordinary consumers. Chief executive Colin Angle frames the goal as making housework optional: people who choose not to clean will have an automatic alternative.

events.title: DARPA Grand Challenge 2004
events.summary: DARPA's retrospective describes the first Grand Challenge, held March 13, 2004, as a prize race for self-driving ground vehicles across the Mojave Desert from outside Barstow, California, to Primm, Nevada. No vehicle finished and the $1 million prize went unclaimed, but DARPA argues the event was not a loss: it built a community of builders, led to the successful 2005 and 2007 challenges, and established the prize-competition model DARPA was reusing in 2014. The agency frames the whole sequence as the start of the autonomous-vehicle work that defense and commercial players were then carrying forward.

events.title: Amazon Mechanical Turk launches
events.summary: Amazon launches Mechanical Turk in beta as a web service that reverses the usual relation between people and computers. Instead of a person asking a computer to do a task, "a computer program could ask a human being to perform a task and return the results," and coordinate many people at once. Amazon calls this "Artificial Artificial Intelligence": software developers call an API, and behind it paid people do the tasks computers still do badly, such as identifying objects in photographs. The FAQ adds the business case: work that was not worth organizing a staff for becomes affordable when fixed labor costs turn into per-task payments.

events.title: ImageNet dataset
events.summary: ImageNet: taxonomy + global annotation labour + competition
events.sourceNote: The data that transformed AI research-and possibly the world

events.title: Hinton's deep belief nets
events.summary: Hinton, Osindero and Teh argue that networks with many hidden layers can be trained efficiently if they are built "one layer at a time." Each layer is learned as a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) on the output of the layer below, using a "fast, greedy algorithm"; the whole stack is then fine-tuned with a slower "up-down" algorithm, a contrastive version of the wake-sleep algorithm. The result is a generative model of handwritten digits and their labels that, the authors say, "gives better digit classification than the best discriminative learning algorithms." They present the method as evidence for generative, unsupervised learning in deep networks.
events.sourceNote: A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets

events.title: Netflix Prize launches
events.summary: Netflix opened a public contest on October 2, 2006 to improve Cinematch, its movie recommendation system. It released more than 100 million customer ratings and offered $1,000,000 to the first team whose predictions beat Cinematch's accuracy by 10 percent on a withheld test set, plus a $50,000 Progress Prize each year. Accuracy was defined as root mean squared error (RMSE) between predicted and actual star ratings. The rules attach conditions to winning: the team must share its method with Netflix, grant Netflix a non-exclusive license, and "describe to the world" how the method works. The FAQ explains the design choices and admits what the single metric leaves out.

events.title: NVIDIA announces CUDA
events.summary: NVIDIA announces CUDA, "a fundamentally new architecture for computing on NVIDIA graphics processing units," together with what it calls the industry's first C compiler for the GPU. The company's claim is that a graphics chip can now work as a general computer: hundreds of processor cores communicate and cooperate on one problem, "up to 100 times faster than traditional approaches." The press release pitches this to product designers, data analysts, technical computing and game physics, and ships it on a new gaming card, the GeForce 8800.

events.title: Common Crawl founded
events.summary: Common Crawl is a nonprofit that crawls the web and gives away the results. Its 2011 blog post tells the founding story: Gil Elbaz formed the foundation "a little under four years" earlier because he believed an open archive of web crawl data should exist for research and business, and because falling storage and bandwidth costs made it possible. Its current About page tells a second story: the archive, begun in 2008 and now over 10 petabytes, "has become one of the most widely used sources of training data for large language models." The two documents show the same project described first as open-web infrastructure and later as a base layer of generative AI.

events.title: Google self-driving car project
events.summary: Waymo's company history dates its origin to 2009, when Google set itself the challenge of driving autonomously over ten uninterrupted 100-mile routes in Toyota Prius cars. Google's first public account of the project came in Sebastian Thrun's October 2010 blog post. It presents self-driving cars as a way to prevent traffic accidents, free up commuting time and cut emissions "by fundamentally changing car use," and reports that the test cars, always with trained operators on board, had logged over 140,000 miles. Waymo's current page tells the same history as the first steps toward a commercial product: "the world's most trusted driver."

events.title: ImageNet presented at CVPR
events.summary: The Princeton team argues that the flood of images on the internet could support better vision algorithms, but only if it is organized. They introduce ImageNet, an image database built on the noun hierarchy of WordNet, aiming for 500–1,000 clean, full-resolution images for each of WordNet's roughly 80,000 noun concepts ("synsets"). The paper reports the database at about 10% of that goal (12 subtrees, 5,247 synsets, 3.2 million images) and argues it is already larger, more accurate and more diverse than existing datasets. It describes how the images were cleaned by paid workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk, and hopes ImageNet will become a training resource and a "new and challenging benchmark dataset."
events.sourceNote: ImageNet - A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database

events.title: IBM Watson wins Jeopardy!
events.summary: On February 16, 2011, the producers of Jeopardy! announced that IBM's Watson had won the first "man vs. machine" competition on the show, beating its two most successful players, Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter. IBM's own history page presents the win as a leap in natural language processing: a question-answering system that could understand questions in ordinary language and answer them "far more accurately than any standard search technology," without an internet connection. IBM then presents Watson's later business uses as the continuation of that victory.

events.title: Apple unveils Siri with iPhone 4S
events.summary: Apple's press release announces the iPhone 4S and folds Siri into a list of hardware and software features: a dual-core A5 chip, a new camera, 1080p video, iOS 5 and iCloud. Siri is presented as "an intelligent assistant that helps you get things done just by asking." The release claims Siri understands context and natural speech, draws on personal data the user allows it to access (contacts, location), and carries out everyday tasks such as calls, messages, reminders, search and directions. Apple frames the phone as a combination that competitors cannot copy with a feature checklist.

events.title: Google Brain's cat paper
events.summary: The authors ask whether a network can learn to detect high-level concepts, such as faces, from images that nobody has labeled. They answer yes, and they locate the reason earlier work failed in scale: datasets, models and training runs had been kept small so that training finished in a practical time. By scaling all three at once (10 million YouTube frames, a network with 1 billion parameters, 1,000 machines for three days), they obtain single neurons that respond to faces, cat faces and human bodies, and features that set a new result on ImageNet's 22,000-category task.
events.sourceNote: Building High-level Features Using Large Scale Unsupervised Learning

events.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
events.summary: AlexNet wins; deep learning becomes the paradigm
events.sourceNote: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

events.title: word2vec
events.summary: Four Google researchers propose two simple architectures, Continuous Bag-of-Words (CBOW) and Skip-gram, for learning a vector for every word from very large text collections. They drop the non-linear hidden layer that makes neural language models expensive, trading some expressive power for the ability to train on billions of words. They introduce a test set of about 19,500 word-relationship questions and report that vectors trained this way answer them far better than earlier published vectors, at much lower cost: less than a day for 1.6 billion words.
events.sourceNote: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

events.title: Generative adversarial nets
events.summary: The authors propose a new way to train generative models: set two networks against each other. A generator G tries to produce samples resembling the training data; a discriminator D tries to tell real data from G's output. G is trained to make D wrong. The authors frame this as a two-player minimax game and prove that, given enough capacity, it has a unique solution in which G reproduces the data distribution and D can do no better than a coin flip. Because both players can be ordinary multilayer networks, the whole system trains with backpropagation, without the Markov chains or approximate inference that earlier deep generative models required.

events.title: Amazon Echo and Alexa launch
events.summary: On November 6, 2014, Amazon launched the Echo, a speaker controlled by voice and woken by the name "Alexa," whose processing ran on Amazon Web Services. The launch report describes an invitation-only device that answers questions and plays music, and that Amazon said would keep learning: "The more you use Echo, the more it adapts to your speech patterns, vocabulary, and personal preferences." Five years later, Alexa's head scientist Rohit Prasad presented the Echo as the start of "voice-enabled ambient computing," which he says shifted "the cognitive load from customers to AI," and described how Alexa grew from zero interactions to billions per week by combining deep learning with AWS's data and compute.

events.title: TensorFlow open-sourced
events.summary: Google announces that it is releasing TensorFlow, its second-generation machine learning system, as open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Pichai presents it as the system behind speech recognition in the Google app, Smart Reply in Inbox and search in Google Photos, and argues that opening it will let researchers, engineers and hobbyists exchange ideas "through working code rather than just research papers." Dean and Monga explain the engineering reason: the first-generation system, DistBelief, was too tied to Google's internal infrastructure to share, and TensorFlow was built to be general, portable and production-ready.

events.title: ResNet
events.summary: Four Microsoft Research authors report that adding layers to a deep network can make it worse on its own training data, a "degradation problem" that is not overfitting but a failure of optimization. They propose residual learning: each small stack of layers learns only the difference from its input, which is carried forward unchanged by a shortcut connection. The change adds no parameters and no computation, and it lets them train networks of 152 layers on ImageNet and over 1,000 on CIFAR-10. An ensemble of these networks won the ILSVRC 2015 classification task with 3.57% top-5 error.
events.sourceNote: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

events.title: OpenAI founded as a nonprofit
events.summary: Read together, these three documents are OpenAI's own record of restructuring itself twice in four years while insisting the mission never changed. The 2015 announcement founds OpenAI as a nonprofit "unconstrained by a need to generate financial return." The 2018 Charter keeps that language of benefit to humanity but adds, for the first time, a public acknowledgment that the lab anticipates needing to "marshal substantial resources" to fulfill its mission. The 2019 OpenAI LP post resolves that tension institutionally: OpenAI creates a capped-profit for-profit subsidiary, controlled by the original nonprofit board, so it can raise investment capital while still claiming the nonprofit's mission as OpenAI LP's "primary fiduciary obligation".

events.title: AlphaGo
events.summary: a benchmark ends a public argument
events.sourceNote: Mastering the game of Go with deepneural networks and tree search

events.title: Microsoft withdraws Tay
events.summary: Peter Lee of Microsoft apologizes for "the unintended offensive and hurtful tweets from Tay," a chatbot Microsoft launched on Twitter that Wednesday, and explains that Tay is offline. He attributes the failure to "a coordinated attack by a subset of people" who exploited a vulnerability Microsoft had not anticipated, while taking "full responsibility for not seeing this possibility ahead of time." He argues that the challenges of AI design are "just as much social as they are technical," and that doing AI right requires iterating in public, with caution, and learning from mistakes.

events.title: Concrete Problems in AI Safety
events.summary: Six researchers from Google Brain, Stanford, UC Berkeley and OpenAI argue that AI safety can be studied as a set of practical machine learning problems rather than through speculation about superintelligence. They define "accidents" as unintended and harmful behavior that emerges from poor design of real-world AI systems, and they sort accident risk into five research problems: avoiding negative side effects, avoiding reward hacking, scalable oversight, safe exploration, and robustness to distributional shift. They argue that trends toward reinforcement learning, more complex environments and more autonomous systems will make these problems more important, and they propose experiments for each.

events.title: Partnership on AI announced
events.summary: Amazon, DeepMind/Google, Facebook, IBM and Microsoft announced a non-profit, the Partnership on Artificial Intelligence to Benefit People and Society, to "advance public understanding" of AI and "formulate best practices" on its challenges. The press release promises research and best-practice recommendations published under an open license, in areas from ethics and fairness to privacy and the reliability of AI systems. The founding firms fund it and say they will share leadership with independent parties, with equal corporate and non-corporate representation on the board. The release states that the organization does not intend to lobby government. DeepMind's post frames the effort as building "new models of open collaboration and accountability" around a technology it expects to have major positive impact.

events.title: Obama White House AI report
events.summary: The report surveys "the current state of AI, its existing and potential applications, and the questions that are raised for society and public policy by progress in AI," and closes with 23 numbered recommendations to federal agencies. It is not a request for legislation. It asks agencies to study, monitor, coordinate, and report — on open training data, on regulatory expertise, on workforce diversity, on autonomous weapons policy — rather than proposing anything Congress would need to pass. The document is explicit that AI's economic effects, safety risks, and fairness questions are all still open, and that the government's role for now is to convene, monitor, and prepare rather than to decide.
events.sourceNote: "Preparing for the Future of Artificial Intelligence"

events.title: Transformer (Attention Is All You Need)
events.summary: translation architecture, later reinterpreted

events.title: Asilomar AI Principles
events.summary: The Future of Life Institute (FLI) presents 23 principles developed at its Beneficial AI 2017 conference in Asilomar, meant to state "the AI community's shared vision for AI, should it exist." The principles fall into three groups: research issues (the goal should be "beneficial intelligence," with funding for research on beneficial use, cooperation among developers and race avoidance); ethics and values (safety, transparency, responsibility, value alignment, privacy, shared benefit, human control, avoiding an arms race in lethal autonomous weapons); and longer-term issues (capability caution, catastrophic and existential risk, recursive self-improvement, superintelligence for the common good). FLI says each principle had support from at least 90% of conference participants and that the list has become one of the most influential sets of AI governance principles.

events.title: DeepMind's missing ethics board
events.summary: Three years after Google's 2014 acquisition of DeepMind, this Guardian article investigates an ethics and safety board Google reportedly agreed to establish as a condition of the deal. The board's existence was never confirmed at the time of the acquisition, became public only through a leak to a trade publication, and has never had its membership, meetings, or activity disclosed despite repeated requests. The article contrasts this with a separate, public ethics board DeepMind created for its health-data partnerships, and quotes early investor Jaan Tallinn and philosopher Nick Bostrom on why such a board matters and why its quiet operation might be defensible.
events.sourceNote: "Whatever happened to the DeepMind AI ethics board Google promised"

events.title: Gender Shades
events.summary: Buolamwini and Gebru argue that the accuracy of commercial facial analysis cannot be judged by a single aggregate number. They show that two widely used face benchmarks, IJB-A and Adience, are mostly made up of lighter-skinned people, build a new benchmark balanced by gender and skin type, and use it to audit three commercial gender classifiers sold by Microsoft, IBM and Face++. All three perform worst on darker-skinned women, with error rates up to 34.7%, against at most 0.8% for lighter-skinned men. The authors conclude that inclusive benchmarks and subgroup accuracy reports are needed before companies can claim fair, transparent and accountable facial analysis.

events.title: Datasheets for Datasets
events.summary: The authors argue that machine learning has "no standardized process for documenting machine learning datasets," even though a dataset's characteristics shape how models behave, including whether they reproduce societal biases. They propose that every dataset be accompanied by a datasheet documenting its motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing, uses, distribution and maintenance. The goal is for dataset creators to reflect carefully on how they make and share data, and for dataset consumers to have the information they need to choose data and avoid misuse. The authors explicitly state that the datasheet process should not be automated.

events.title: MLPerf benchmarks
events.summary: MLPerf's founders argue that machine learning needs industry-standard benchmarks to compare the fast-growing number of hardware and software systems for training neural networks. The May 2018 launch announces a suite that measures the time it takes to train models to perform tasks such as recognizing objects, translating languages and playing Go. The 2020 paper explains why this is harder than earlier computing benchmarks: speed-ups can lower model quality, training is random, and systems differ so much that identical code and settings are hard to impose. MLPerf answers with a "time to train" to a fixed quality target, reference implementations, and rules about what submitters may change.

events.title: Google Duplex demo
events.summary: Google announces Duplex, a system that makes phone calls to businesses on a user's behalf to carry out narrow tasks such as booking a hair salon appointment or a restaurant table. Leviathan and Matias argue that automated phone systems force callers to adapt to the machine, and that Duplex reverses this by sounding natural enough that people can "speak normally, like they would to another person, without having to adapt to a machine." They say the key to this was restricting Duplex to closed domains, and that it cannot hold general conversations. They say transparency about the call's intent matters and that Google will experiment with the right approach.

events.title: Google's 2018 AI principles
events.summary: Google publishes seven principles meant to "actively govern" its AI research and product decisions — social benefit, avoiding unfair bias, safety, accountability, privacy, scientific excellence, and restricting use to purposes consistent with the principles — plus four categories of application it says it will not pursue, including weapons whose principal purpose is to injure people. The post frames this as a response to AI's growing reach into society and presents the principles as continuous with commitments made in Google's 2004 Founders' Letter. The cached page itself carries a later editorial note, dated February 4, 2025, saying the principles have since been updated; that note is a fact about the page's later history, not part of the 2018 text analyzed here.

events.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
events.summary: The authors argue that there are "no standardized documentation procedures" for communicating how trained machine learning models perform, and that this matters most when models are used in health care, employment, education and law enforcement. They propose model cards: short documents released with trained models that report benchmarked evaluation broken down by cultural, demographic and phenotypic groups and their intersections, along with intended uses, out-of-scope uses, evaluation data, ethical considerations and caveats. They present model cards as a complement to Datasheets for Datasets and as "a step towards the responsible democratization of machine learning."

events.title: BERT
events.summary: Four Google AI Language researchers argue that existing pre-trained language models are held back by reading text in one direction only. BERT removes that limit with a "masked language model" objective: hide some words and train a Transformer encoder to predict them from context on both sides. Pre-trained once on unlabeled text, the same model can be fine-tuned with one added output layer for question answering, inference and classification, and it sets new state-of-the-art results on eleven language tasks, including a GLUE score of 80.5.
events.sourceNote: BERT - Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding

events.title: PyTorch 1.0 released
events.summary: Facebook releases PyTorch 1.0 stable at the NeurIPS conference, presenting it as a framework that takes AI "from research prototyping to production deployment." The May 2018 roadmap explains the problem 1.0 was built to solve: PyTorch was popular with researchers for its Python integration and flexibility, but weak at "production-support," while Facebook's production framework, Caffe2, already ran in its datacenters and on over a billion phones. Facebook's answer was to "marry PyTorch and Caffe2," adding a just-in-time compiler that turns Python models into a form that can run without Python, while promising researchers that existing code would keep working.

events.title: EO 13859: American AI leadership
events.summary: The order establishes the "American AI Initiative," guided by five principles that pair promotion with protection: drive technological breakthroughs, reduce barriers to deployment, train the workforce, foster public trust, and promote an international environment while "protecting our critical AI technologies from acquisition by strategic competitors and adversarial nations." Operationally, it is short: it instructs named agency heads to prioritize AI in budgets, review federal data for wider AI research access, draft a regulatory-guidance memorandum, produce a NIST standards plan, and prepare a classified action plan to protect the U.S. AI advantage — each on a fixed deadline (90, 120, or 180 days) but without appropriating money or creating enforceable rights.
events.sourceNote: Executive Order 13859 - Maintaining American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence

events.title: OpenAI's GPT-2 staged release
events.summary: OpenAI announces GPT-2, a 1.5-billion-parameter transformer language model trained "simply to predict the next word in 40GB of Internet text," which generates coherent paragraphs and performs reading comprehension, translation, question answering and summarization without task-specific training. Because of "concerns about malicious applications of the technology," OpenAI withholds the full trained model, dataset and training code, and releases only a much smaller model and a technical paper. It calls this "an experiment in responsible disclosure" and says the AI community will need to develop publication norms. A May 2019 update formalizes the approach as "staged release" and "partnership-based sharing."

events.title: San Francisco bans face recognition
events.summary: On May 14, 2019, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors passed the Stop Secret Surveillance Ordinance, authored by Supervisor Aaron Peskin. The ACLU of Northern California and the coalition behind the law present it as doing two things: bringing "accountability and oversight to surveillance technology" in general, and making San Francisco "the first city in the United States to prohibit government use of face surveillance systems." The coalition argues that face recognition in government hands would expand state power to track people, "supercharge discriminatory policing," and entangle residents with immigration enforcement, and that the right answer is democratic control before adoption rather than rules after deployment.

events.title: OECD AI Principles adopted
events.summary: The OECD Council adopted its Recommendation on Artificial Intelligence at its ministerial meeting on May 22, 2019, calling it "the first intergovernmental standard on AI." The Recommendation sets out five values-based principles for "responsible stewardship of trustworthy AI" (inclusive growth and well-being; rule of law, human rights and democratic values; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; accountability) and five recommendations to governments (R&D investment, an enabling ecosystem, an interoperable policy environment, labour-market preparation, international co-operation). Its premise is that trust is what lets AI spread: the Council treats trustworthiness as "a key factor for the diffusion and adoption of AI." The cached text is the 2024 revision, so the principle wording quoted below is the current version, not necessarily the 2019 wording.

events.title: Hao's inside account of OpenAI
events.summary: Based on three days at OpenAI's office and nearly three dozen interviews, Hao reports a gap between OpenAI's public self-description as an open, mission-driven nonprofit and what she found operating behind closed doors: a culture of secrecy, tight message control, a 2018 Charter used internally as a loyalty test tied to pay, and a still-unexplained shift toward the compute-heavy, increasingly closed research strategy that produced the withheld GPT-2 release and a secret "top-secret" follow-on project. She frames OpenAI's nonprofit status and its later 2019 for-profit transition as decisions made under competitive and financial pressure that the public announcements did not fully disclose.
events.sourceNote: "The messy, secretive reality behind OpenAI's bid to save the world"

events.title: 80 Million Tiny Images withdrawn
events.summary: On June 29, 2020, the creators of the 80 Million Tiny Images dataset at MIT withdrew it. Their notice says the dataset "contains some derogatory terms as categories and offensive images," a result of "the automated data collection procedure that relied on nouns from WordNet." Because the images were too many and too small to inspect by hand, they decided removal was the only reliable fix: the dataset was taken offline for good, and they asked researchers to stop using it and delete their copies. The notice credits a preprint by Vinay Prabhu and Abeba Birhane, which argued that large vision datasets inherited offensive categories from WordNet and were built from images of people collected without consent.

events.title: MMLU benchmark
events.summary: Hendrycks and colleagues argue that existing language benchmarks no longer measure what large pretrained models can actually do. GLUE and SuperGLUE were each matched at human level within about a year, yet the authors hold that models remain far from human language understanding "as a whole." Their answer is a 57-subject multiple-choice test, from elementary mathematics to professional law and medicine, taken only in zero-shot and few-shot settings, so that it measures knowledge picked up during pretraining rather than skill at a fine-tuning set. The result they report: most models sit at random chance, the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 reaches 43.9%, and no model reaches expert level on any subject.

events.title: Timnit Gebru forced out of Google
events.summary: MIT Technology Review reports that on December 2, 2020, Timnit Gebru, co-lead of Google's ethical AI team, announced that Google had forced her out, and that the exit came out of a conflict over a draft paper on the risks of large language models. The article summarizes that paper's four risks (environmental and financial cost, training data too large to document, research effort diverted from understanding, and text that can fool people) and sets them against Google's reasons for objecting: Jeff Dean said the paper "didn't meet our bar for publication" and ignored relevant research. The piece presents both sides but gives space to critics who argue Google pushed her out over findings inconvenient to a core line of its research.
events.sourceNote: Timnit Gebru forced out of Google

events.title: Stochastic Parrots
events.summary: The paper argues that the NLP field's post-2018 turn toward ever-larger language models should not be narrated simply as technical progress. Larger models improve benchmark performance, but they also create environmental costs, access barriers, documentation debt, bias amplification, misleading claims about understanding, and downstream social harms.
events.sourceNote: "On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots - Can Language Models Be Too Big"

events.title: OpenAI's CLIP
events.summary: OpenAI announces CLIP (Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training), a model that learns visual concepts from text paired with images found on the internet rather than from hand-labeled datasets. Because it is trained to match images with captions, CLIP can be turned into a classifier for almost any set of categories by naming them in plain language, with no task-specific training examples. OpenAI argues that this makes CLIP's benchmark scores more honest: a model that never trains on a benchmark cannot "cheat" on it, so its performance there better predicts its performance elsewhere.

events.title: OpenAI's DALL·E
events.summary: OpenAI announces DALL·E, a 12-billion-parameter version of GPT-3 trained to generate images from text descriptions using text–image pairs. The post argues that "manipulating visual concepts through language is now within reach" and demonstrates this through a long series of captions: anthropomorphized animals and objects, combinations of unrelated concepts, rendered text, changes of viewpoint and style, and transformations of existing images. It is a research announcement with curated examples, not a product release; the post says OpenAI plans to study the model's economic impact, bias and ethical challenges in the future.

events.title: NSCAI final report
events.summary: The Commission concludes that "the United States needs to implement a strategy to defend and compete in the AI era," organized in two parts: defending against AI-enabled threats (Part I) and winning the broader technology competition with China (Part II). Its central factual claim is that China "possesses the might, talent, and ambition to surpass the United States as the world's leader in AI in the next decade if current trends do not change," and its central policy claim is that only a "White House–led strategy," backed by tens of billions in new federal spending — $40 billion for AI R&D, up to $35 billion for domestic microelectronics — can prevent that outcome.

events.title: EU proposes the AI Act
events.summary: The Commission proposes binding EU-wide rules for AI systems, built on a risk tier rather than a technology definition: certain practices are prohibited outright, "high-risk" systems face mandatory conformity requirements and ex-ante assessment before they can reach the market, a narrow set of systems face transparency-only obligations, and everything else is unregulated apart from voluntary codes of conduct. Unlike the U.S. documents drafted for this course week, this is a Regulation — directly applicable law under Article 288 TFEU, chosen specifically "for a uniform application of the new rules" rather than an advisory report or an executive order.

events.title: Anthropic's founding raise
events.summary: The 2021 press release announces a $124 million Series A for Anthropic, led by Jaan Tallinn and joined by Dustin Moskovitz and Eric Schmidt among others, to fund research into "reliable and steerable AI systems." The 2023 essay, written after Anthropic had shipped Claude, lays out the company's account of why it exists: rapid AI progress is likely within a decade, nobody yet knows how to make powerful systems reliably safe, and Anthropic's answer is an empirically driven, "portfolio" approach across several safety research directions, pursued on frontier-scale models because the company argues smaller models cannot expose the problems that matter.

events.title: GitHub Copilot preview
events.summary: GitHub launches a limited technical preview of GitHub Copilot, "a new AI pair programmer" that suggests whole lines or entire functions inside the code editor. It is built with OpenAI and runs on OpenAI Codex, which GitHub describes as more capable than GPT-3 at code generation because it was trained on much more public source code. The accompanying FAQ answers the questions GitHub expected: what it was trained on, whether it copies code, who owns the output, what data it collects, and what it means for developer jobs.

events.title: Stanford's foundation-models report
events.summary: A group of more than 100 Stanford researchers, led by Percy Liang and Rishi Bommasani, argues that AI is "undergoing a paradigm shift" toward models trained on broad data at scale and then adapted to many downstream tasks, and names these models "foundation models." Their significance, the report says, comes down to two words: emergence (behavior that is induced by training rather than built) and homogenization (a few models becoming the base for many applications). Homogenization gives leverage but means defects are "inherited by all the adapted models downstream," and because model building has moved almost entirely into industry, the authors argue that academia, with its range of disciplines and non-commercial incentives, must help set the norms for how these models are built and deployed.
events.sourceNote: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models

events.title: UNESCO AI ethics recommendation
events.summary: UNESCO's General Conference adopts a values-and-principles instrument on AI ethics — the organization's own summary calls it "UNESCO's first-ever global standard on AI ethics" — and recommends that member states apply it "on a voluntary basis." The text sets out values (human rights and dignity, environmental flourishing, diversity, peaceful societies), ten principles (proportionality, safety, fairness, privacy, human oversight, transparency, responsibility, awareness, and multi-stakeholder governance), and eight policy action areas member states are asked to consider, from ethical impact assessment to gender and culture.
events.sourceNote: "Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence"

events.title: InstructGPT and RLHF
events.summary: This paper introduces InstructGPT: GPT-3 models fine-tuned to follow written instructions using supervised demonstrations and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). The important historical move is that scale alone is explicitly separated from usefulness: the paper argues that next-token pretraining produces capability, but not necessarily instruction-following, truthfulness, harmlessness, or alignment with user intent.
events.sourceNote: "Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback"

events.title: C2PA provenance spec 1.0
events.summary: The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) announces version 1.0 of its technical specification for digital provenance, which it calls the first industry standard of its kind. The specification defines how information about who created or changed a piece of digital content, and how it was altered, can be attached to images, video, audio and documents in a tamper-evident way. The coalition presents it as a response to the difficulty of trusting online content, naming "deepfakes generated by artificial intelligence" alongside traditionally manipulated media, and designs it as an opt-in open standard for software, devices, platforms and regulators to adopt.

events.title: LAION-5B released
events.summary: LAION announces an openly available dataset of 5.85 billion image-text pairs, fourteen times larger than its earlier LAION-400M. The post argues that large image-text models such as CLIP, DALL-E, ALIGN and FLORENCE were trained on billions of pairs that no one outside a few large groups could access, and that an open dataset at this scale lets a broad research community study and train such models. LAION releases the data "for research purposes," warns that it is uncurated and may contain disturbing content, and says it does not recommend using it to build ready-to-go industrial products.

events.title: BIG-bench
events.summary: BIG-bench (the Beyond the Imitation Game benchmark) is a set of 204 tasks written by 450 authors at 132 institutions, meant to test language models on problems "believed to be beyond the capabilities of current language models." The authors argue that existing benchmarks are too narrow, saturate too quickly and rely on non-expert labeling, so they cannot predict what larger models will do. BIG-bench is built to measure how performance changes with scale. The main findings: performance and calibration improve with size but stay poor compared with human raters; model families behave much alike; some tasks improve smoothly while others show "breakthrough" jumps at a critical scale; and social bias often grows with scale in ambiguous contexts.

events.title: Stable Diffusion public release
events.summary: Stability AI announces that Stable Diffusion, a text-to-image model already released to researchers, is now public: the weights, model card and code are downloadable from Hugging Face, with a hosted demo, a development notebook and Stability's own DreamStudio service alongside. The company presents the release as the product of weeks spent ensuring "a safe and ethical release," resting on two measures: a permissive licence that places responsibility for ethical and legal use on whoever runs the model, and an AI-based safety classifier switched on by default whose settings users can change. Stability describes the result as "a single file that compresses the visual information of humanity into a few gigabytes."

events.title: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights
events.summary: OSTP sets out five principles meant to guide "the design, use, and deployment of automated systems to protect the rights of the American public" in the age of artificial intelligence: safe and effective systems, algorithmic discrimination protections, data privacy, notice and explanation, and human alternatives with fallback. The document states its own limits directly: it "is non-binding and does not constitute U.S. government policy," and it "does not supersede, modify, or direct an interpretation of any existing statute, regulation, policy, or international instrument."
events.sourceNote: "Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights"

events.title: US chip export controls
events.summary: The Bureau of Industry and Security's interim final rule amends the Export Administration Regulations to block China's access to advanced AI chips, the chip-design software used to create them, and the manufacturing equipment used to fabricate them, plus a fourth control on the equipment used to build that manufacturing equipment. Announced October 7, 2022, seven weeks before ChatGPT's public release, the rule is not a response to a consumer AI product; it targets supercomputing and military-modernization capability directly. Allen's CSIS analysis, published four days later, argues the rule's four provisions interlock into a single strategy of controlling technological "chokepoints" across the semiconductor supply chain, rather than four separate, independent measures.
events.sourceNote: BIS October 2022 export controls on advanced computing

events.title: Stanford's HELM
events.summary: Stanford's Center for Research on Foundation Models argues that language models have become the base of most language technologies while their "capabilities, limitations, and risks are not well understood," and that the field needs to benchmark them "holistically." HELM does three things: it lays out a taxonomy of scenarios and metrics and says openly what it leaves out; it measures seven metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, efficiency) rather than accuracy alone; and it runs 30 models from 12 organizations under the same prompts and conditions. The authors present HELM as "a living benchmark for the community."

events.title: ChatGPT launch
events.summary: OpenAI's launch post presents ChatGPT as a dialogue-oriented sibling of InstructGPT, trained through reinforcement learning from human feedback and released as a research preview. The post's historical importance is that it frames ChatGPT not as a sudden invention, but as an incremental product of GPT-3.5, InstructGPT, supervised dialogue data, reward modeling, PPO, user feedback, and iterative deployment.

events.title: Historians' genealogy of AI and power
events.summary: historians turn the STS toolkit on AI
events.sourceNote: “Histories of Artificial Intelligence, A Genealogy of Power”

events.title: LLaMA released
events.summary: The article argues that Meta's LLaMA changed the large language model landscape by making a powerful foundation model available for research use in multiple sizes, including smaller models that required less computing infrastructure to study, retrain, and fine-tune. Its central historical problem is access: by early 2023, large language models had become technically important but institutionally concentrated because only a small number of organizations could afford to train and operate them. Meta presents LLaMA as a way to widen research participation while still managing risk through controlled, noncommercial access.
events.sourceNote: Introducing LLaMA - A foundational 65-billion-parameter large language model

events.title: China's deep synthesis rules
events.summary: Three Chinese state bodies (the cyberspace administration, the industry and information technology ministry, and public security) place "deep synthesis" technology, meaning generative systems that create text, images, audio, video or virtual scenes, inside the existing regime for internet information services. The rules make service providers responsible for what their users generate. Providers must verify users' real identities, review both inputs and outputs, label synthetic content, run security assessments on face and voice tools, and file with regulators if their services have "public opinion properties or the capacity for social mobilization." The stated purposes include national security, the public interest and to "carry forward the Core Socialist Values."

events.title: NIST AI RMF 1.0
events.summary: NIST offers organizations a voluntary framework for managing the risks of AI systems, organized around four functions — GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE — and built on seven characteristics of trustworthy AI, including "valid and reliable," "explainable and interpretable," and "fair with their harmful biases managed." The document does not set a technical standard or a compliance bar; it is explicit that it does neither.

events.title: Getty sues Stability AI (Delaware)
events.summary: Getty Images, the stock-photo licensor, sues Stability AI in federal court in Delaware, where Stability AI, Inc. is incorporated. Getty alleges that Stability copied more than 12 million photographs from Getty's websites, with their captions and metadata, to train the image generator Stable Diffusion, without a license and against the sites' terms of use. It adds that Stable Diffusion's outputs often carry a distorted Getty watermark, which Getty says confuses buyers about where the images come from and damages its trademarks. The claims are copyright infringement, false and removed copyright management information under 17 U.S.C. § 1202, trademark infringement, unfair competition and dilution under the Lanham Act, and Delaware trade-practice and dilution claims. Getty asks for damages, an injunction, and the destruction of every version of Stable Diffusion trained on its content.
events.sourceNote: Getty Images v Stability AI Delaware complaint

events.title: LLaMA weights leak
events.summary: James Vincent argues that the leak of Meta’s LLaMA model marked a significant moment in the struggle over who should control access to powerful AI systems. The article explains a shift from large language models as guarded corporate or research assets toward models that could circulate through informal online networks, independent researchers, and open-source communities. What mattered was not simply that LLaMA was technically capable, but that its leakage exposed unresolved questions about AI safety, openness, institutional trust, and the political economy of access to expensive computational systems.
events.sourceNote: Meta’s powerful AI language model has leaked online — what happens now?

events.title: GPT-4 technical report
events.summary: OpenAI presents GPT-4 as "a large-scale, multimodal model" that accepts images and text and produces text, and that "exhibits human-level performance on various professional and academic benchmarks," passing a simulated bar exam "with a score around the top 10% of test takers." The report's main technical claim concerns predictability: OpenAI says it built infrastructure that let it forecast parts of GPT-4's performance from models trained with far less compute. It also states what it will not disclose. Citing "the competitive landscape and the safety implications," the report gives no details on architecture, model size, hardware, training compute, dataset construction or training method.

events.title: The pause letter
events.summary: Two months apart, two civil-society interventions took opposite rhetorical approaches to the same underlying worry. The Future of Life Institute's open letter calls on "all AI labs to immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4," backing that specific demand with roughly twenty paragraphs of argument, footnoted citations, and a list of governance measures. The Center for AI Safety's statement, published ten weeks later, makes no specific demand at all — it asks signatories to agree only that mitigating AI extinction risk should be a global priority, alongside risks like pandemics and nuclear war. The pause was not observed by any major lab; the statement, asking for far less, was signed by a wide range of researchers and public figures.

events.title: UK pro-innovation AI white paper
events.summary: The UK government proposes to regulate AI without a new AI law or a new AI regulator. Five cross-sector principles will be issued "on a non-statutory basis and implemented by existing regulators," each applying them within its own domain, while new "central functions" inside government monitor risks and coordinate. The approach is "context-specific": rules attach to the outcomes of particular uses, not to sectors or technologies. A statutory duty on regulators may follow "when parliamentary time allows," but only if monitoring shows it is needed. For foundation models, the paper concludes it "would be premature to take specific regulatory action."

events.title: Italy suspends ChatGPT
events.summary: Italy's data protection authority orders OpenAI L.L.C., as a matter of urgency, to provisionally limit the processing of personal data of persons located in Italy, effective immediately upon receipt of the order. The order is written entirely in the register of data-protection law: it does not evaluate ChatGPT as an AI system in the abstract, but finds specific violations of named articles of the GDPR — the absence of any privacy notice to users and data subjects, the absence of a legal basis for using personal data to train the model, factual inaccuracy in the data ChatGPT processes about individuals, and the absence of any age-verification mechanism despite a stated 13-plus age requirement.

events.title: Brain and DeepMind merge
events.summary: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis's memo to staff, republished as a blog post, announces that DeepMind and the Brain team from Google Research are merging into a single unit, Google DeepMind, under his leadership. He frames the merger as necessary to "work with greater speed, stronger collaboration and execution" and to build AGI "safely and responsibly," and names the new leadership structure — himself as CEO, Eli Collins as VP of Product, Zoubin Ghahramani joining research leadership under Koray Kavukcuoglu, and a new Scientific Board still being finalized. The memo does not explain why the two organizations, which had operated separately for over a decade, needed to merge now.

events.title: Open LLM Leaderboard
events.summary: Hugging Face ran the Open LLM Leaderboard as "a public leaderboard comparing open access large language models." About six weeks after the first public discussions on the Space, the team published this post to explain why LLaMA's MMLU score on the leaderboard was far below the number in Meta's paper. Their answer is that a benchmark name does not fix a measurement: three implementations of the same MMLU questions (the original Berkeley code, Stanford's HELM, and EleutherAI's Evaluation Harness) differ in prompt format and in how they read an answer out of the model, and they produce different scores and even different model rankings. The authors conclude that evaluations are "strongly tied to their implementations" and that open, standardized, reproducible evaluation libraries are what make comparison possible.

events.title: Google 'No Moat' memo
events.summary: The article republishes and contextualizes a leaked internal Google document arguing that the decisive shift in large language models in early 2023 was not simply OpenAI versus Google, but the rapid rise of open-source and semi-open AI development. The leaked author claims that cheaper fine-tuning methods, smaller models, quantization, leaked model weights, and distributed experimentation had undermined the assumption that frontier AI advantage depended mainly on enormous proprietary models and corporate secrecy. Historically, the article tries to explain why the center of AI innovation appeared to move, at least temporarily, from large firms with massive compute budgets toward a broader ecosystem of researchers, hobbyists, universities, startups, and open-source communities.
events.sourceNote: Google We Have No Moat And Neither Does OpenAI

events.title: Senate AI oversight hearing
events.summary: At the first in a planned series of hearings, the Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, and the Law heard from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, NYU professor emeritus Gary Marcus, and IBM chief privacy and trust officer Christina Montgomery on how, or whether, to regulate generative AI.
